High –energy ball milling of W –6.3Ni–2.7Cu–1Sn (wt. %) powder was performed in a planetary ball mill (QM –1SP4) in the alcohol medium using tungsten carbide balls as grinding media. The powders were mixed for 20 h in 500 ml stainless steel jars which were filled with argon to minimize oxidation.
Fig. 1. The SEM micrographs of initial powders (a) tungsten, (b) nickel, (c) copper and (d) tin, (e) milled for 20 h.
The milled powder was heated to 1250 °C at a constant rate of 10 °C/min and subsequently cooled at a controlled rate (10 °C/min) in a DSC unit (model: STA449C, supplier: Netzsch, Germany).

Alcohol solution containing 10% zinc stearate was used to lubricate the die wall before compacting. Then the milled powders were compacted into green tensile parts (about 4.5 g) under a H41 –25C type hydraulic presser.
A 0.5 h hold was given at 900 °C to form tungsten skeleton.
The green compacts were sintered for 1 h, a temperature of 1100–1200 °C, and a heating rate of 10 ° C /min.

This is mainly due to the formation of liquid phase that promotes the densification at low sintering t emperature during the sintering process . Generally, the densification kinetics is higher during liquid phase sintering process due to fast diffusion rate and capillary forces.

This could be attributable to grain refinement strengthening. Lower sintering temperature provides more restriction on the growth of W grains. Refined W grains can increase the contact surface between W grains an d matrix phase and impede dislocation movement, thus play a very important role for strengthening the alloys.

High –energy ball milling of W –6.3Ni–2.7Cu–1Sn (wt. %) powder was performed in a planetary ball mill (QM –1SP4) in the alcohol medium using tungsten carbide balls as grinding media. The powders were mixed for 20 h in 500 ml stainless steel jars which were filled with argon to minimize oxidation.
The milled powder was heated to 1250 °C at a constant rate of 10 °C/min and subsequently cooled at a controlled rate (10 °C/min) in a DSC unit (model: STA449C, supplier: Netzsch, Germany).

Alcohol solution containing 10% zinc stearate was used to lubricate the die wall before compacting. Then the milled powders were compacted into green tensile parts (about 4.5 g) under a H41 –25C type hydraulic presser.
A 0.5 h hold was given at 900 °C to form tungsten skeleton.
The green compacts were sintered for 1 h, a temperature of 1100–1200 °C, and a heating rate of 10 ° C /min.
The BCC W phase is seen as major peaks in all the alloys, with two relatively weak peaks in the range of 42.716°–43.793° , 49.181°–50.776° , respectively.
We suggest that these two diffraction peaks are γ–(Ni, W, Cu, Sn) phase.

For the low sintering temperature of 1100 °C (Fig. 5a), the tiny W particles appear in bright areas having an agglomerate structure whereas t he matrix phase displays as darker regions with an irregular shape.
As sintering temperature rises to 1150 ° C (see Fig. 5c), the liquid phase forms (according to DSC analysis shown in Fig. 3) and the W grains size increase and become spherical.
